memory: I've always been fascinated by the idea of exploring new places, and that's something I've tried to do whenever my schedule allows. Since I'm a fourth-year Computer Science major, I have to be pretty strategic about planning my trips—between classes, research, campus clubs, and even everyday stuff like heading to the gym or working on group projects, my calendar gets ridiculously cramped. But I've managed to squeeze in some adventures that have given me some of my favorite memories so far.I remember thinking how strange yet thrilling it was to disconnect from my usual coding mindset and focus fully on the wind, the tide charts, and the synergy of the boat with nature. Plus, I'll never forget the fresh lobster rolls we got at a small dockside shack—still the best lobster I've ever had.I visited a number of shrines and temples, and even caught a glimpse of geishas quietly walking down a side street near Gion. It was surreal. I remember writing in my journal—I'm sort of a casual diary-keeper—that being in Kyoto felt like stepping back into an older era, where craftsmanship and tradition take center stage. That sense of stillness and reverence left a big impression on me.My favorite spot was probably the area around the Seine River near Notre-Dame, just strolling with a croissant in hand. It felt so relaxed, especially compared to the hustle of London. My dad loves art, so we spent a whole day at the Louvre, but even that didn't feel like enough time. You could probably spend a week in there without seeing everything.We ended up hiking around, telling stories, and just enjoying nature. That trip reminded me how necessary it is to occasionally step away from my laptop and, ironically, it recharged me for the programming tasks waiting for me back at campus.I've been eyeing some internships in Silicon Valley for next summer, so if that pans out, I might spend a couple of weeks exploring the West Coast. I've heard great things about Portland, Seattle, and Vancouver—everyone always praises the coffee, craft beer, and beautiful scenery. If I line things up just right, I could do a road trip through Washington and Oregon after my internship ends, maybe with a friend or two who'll also be interning in the Bay Area. It would be awesome to discover the coastal highways, the Redwood forests, and those hidden beaches I keep seeing in photos. That might be my last chance to have a big chunk of free time before the post-grad grind starts.I have a dog at home, though he's really the family dog since he stays with my parents. He's a Golden Retriever named Archie, and he's super energetic. One time, my family considered taking him on a road trip, but Archie hates being cooped up in a car for too long—he gets fidgety and starts pawing at the windows. So we decided to leave him with my uncle for that trip. Still, I dream of traveling in an RV or camper van, bringing Archie along for hikes and beach runs. It'd be a different type of adventure, but definitely one that'd make for some amazing memories.I feel like each locale has taught me something—Japan gave me a sense of reverence for tradition and efficiency, Maine reminded me how timeless and beautiful nature can be, and Europe opened my eyes to the depth of art and culture spanning centuries. Even short trips nearby campus help me unwind and discover hidden gems in my own area. I love collecting postcards along the way, too—every time I look at them, I'm reminded that there's a big, wide world beyond my bedroom. And the more I see, the more inspired I am, not just for personal enjoyment, but also for the creative problem-solving that goes into my coding projects and research ideas. There's something about experiencing new places that heightens my curiosity and makes me want to explore fresh angles in everything I do.Traveling has become one of those passions I'll keep nurturing even after graduation. I'm anxious to see where my future career in computer science will lead me—I hope to land a job that allows some remote work days or flexible scheduling, so I can keep exploring. Whether it's a weekend trip to a mountain range a few hours away or a flight to a completely different continent, I'm all in. If I ever get the chance to combine my love of coding with my love of travel—like working abroad for a stint or collaborating on an international project—I'd jump at the chance. For now, I'm just enjoying planning the next journey in my head whenever I need a mental break from debugging code. I have a habit of writing down all my tasks, appointments, and deadlines in a planner, so I can see everything laid out in front of me. It helps me prioritize and make sure I don't miss anything important. After checking my schedule, I head to the gym for a quick workout. Exercise is a great way to clear my mind and get energized for the day ahead. I usually spend about an hour at the gym, and then I head back home to get ready for class.I usually have a few classes in the morning, so I need to make sure I'm on time. I try to arrive at each class about 10 minutes early, so I can get settled and ready to go. My favorite classes are the ones that involve coding and problem-solving, as they really challenge me and help me learn new skills. I also make sure to take notes during class, as they're really helpful for studying later on. After my morning classes, I usually grab a quick lunch at the cafeteria or a nearby restaurant. It's a great opportunity to catch up with friends or meet new people. In the afternoons, I often have more classes or study sessions, so I need to stay focused and keep up with the pace. I also try to squeeze in some time for my research projects, as they're really important for my academic development. By the end of the day, I'm usually tired but satisfied with what I've accomplished. I make sure to wind down with some relaxation time, whether it's reading a book, watching a movie, or just hanging out with friends.I have a few more hours of studying and working on my research projects before I can call it a day.
